REGIS REPORT

31 May 2023
 

The Philippines dropped 2.2% in May, retreating after its 1.9% advance in April.  Foreign outflows resumed in May while trading activity remained anemic, with a lack of domestic catalysts and the US debt ceiling issue shaping sentiment. For the first five months of the year, the PSEi is down 1.4%.

CPI inflation in April decelerated to 6.6% from 7.6% in March. The April inflation print came in well below Street expectations (7.2%) and is the slowest rate in eight months. Prices of food (vegetables, fish, and meat) and energy-related items (transport and electricity inflation) continued to decline. The YT-April average inflation rate is at 7.9%. The BSP’s 2023 inflation target at 6.0%.

Unsurprisingly, the BSP kept the policy rate at 6.25% in its May meeting, despite the Fed’s hike earlier in May. The BSP’s decision to pause was not unexpected, given the pronouncements made leading to the meeting. The gap between the BSP policy rate and the US Fed funds rate (5.0% to 5.25%) is at ~1.25%, lower than the historical gap of around 300bp. The BSP  lowered its inflation forecast for 2023 and 2024, suggesting scope for policy rate cuts moving ahead. In the meantime, the BSP looks to be planning a loosening, with a 200bp cut in banks’ regulatory reserve requirement (RRR) seeming imminent.

GDP growth for 1Q was 6.4%, mildly besting market expectations of 6.2%.  On the supply side, the services sector provided the boost to growth.  On the demand side, private consumption grew 6.3% YoY. However, with exports slowing sharply, net imports were a drag.   

The country’s trade deficit for March ballooned to US$4.9bn, taking the 1Q tally to US$14.58bn – up 11% YoY.  The trade deficit continued to deteriorate despite declining commodity prices. Exports continued to drop, contracting 9% in March, albeit at a slower clip than the 18% and 13% drops in Feb and Jan, respectively. Meanwhile, imports fell 2.7% in March, slower than the 11.8% drop in the previous month on the back of lower fuel imports and raw materials. 

The passage of the proposed bill creating the Maharlika Investment Fund (MIF) seems to be getting closer, with the Lower House adopting the Senate version (SB 2020). The bill will be transmitted to the Office of the President for signing into law. Among the provisions of the Senate Bill prohibits the use of funds from the pension funds (GSIS and SSS), Philhealth, Pag-IBIG, OWWA, PVAO in the capitalization of the MIF. The proposed MIF is intended to help bankroll the Marcos administration’s pipeline of 194 infrastructure projects, filling the gaps in infrastructure spending given the government’s tight fiscal position. Infrastructure spend contracted 1% YoY in 1Q23, missing the government’s 6% target. Meanwhile, government debt-to-GDP ratios continued to rise to 61.3% of GDP as of April.  

 
PSEi -2.2% | 6477.36
 
Key data
 

Foreigners turned net sellers  for US$76m in May, bringing the net outflow for the year to $564m. Average daily turnover slightly improved to US$107m mainly due to the MSCi rebalancing. Excluding that event, market turnover was an anemic US$91m/day.

Foreign participation was  higher at 53% vs 50% in April. 

Biggest outflows were seen in MSCi rebalancing names. Deletion MONDE was top sold and saw an outflow of US$22.6m alongside down-weights ALI TEL and JGS. ACEN also was top foreign sold, seeing consistent outflows since the start of the year. Foreigners turned net sellers of ICT after two months of straight inflow.

SMPH surprisingly finished the month top bought despite its down-weight from the MSCI; the stock has been consistently seeing inflow prior to the rebal date alongside MSCi upweight AC. Outside the two, foreign interest remained in banks, mostly in BDO and BPI.

 
LEADERS AND LAGGARDS
 
 

The PSEi’s 147.72-index point decline was broad based, with 22 of 30 index names ending down for the month.

Logging the largest decline in the PSEi was Monde, dropping 13.4% in May, as the stock’s deletion from the MSCI weighed on its performance. Widening losses of Quorn in 1Q also hurt sentiment. In contrast, Jollibee (+4.7% MoM) outperformed on better-than-expected 1Q23 results. The path to recovery for the Philippine business continues, with operating leverage eclipsing persistent pressure from input cost inflation. Meanwhile, the international businesses appear to be turning the corner, and could be further boosted by the China recovery. Meanwhile, Wilcon (-1.9% MoM) and URC (-4.4% MoM) succumbed to profit-taking even as results were seemingly in line with expectations, albeit coming from a higher YoY base.

DNL fell 17.2% for the month. This came after DNL reported 1Q23 had fallen 24% due to a squeeze in oleochemical margins. The imminent opening of its new facility in Batangas could also weigh down profits due to low utilization.

Losses were also led by previous outperformer ICTSI (-10.1% MoM). ICTSI’s shares shed sharply after the company reported organic volumes slipped 0.7% YoY in 1Q23.  Investors largely ignored better-than-expected 1Q23 yield per TEU, as well as indications of a mild improvement in April. Meanwhile, Cebu Air (+6.0% MoM) climbed after reporting its first quarterly profit since the pandemic began.  The business is rapidly recovering, with management upbeat on the prospects of passenger volumes and margins as the business goes back to “normal”.

Also dragging the index were banks BDO and BPI, which dropped 5.6% and 7.1% respectively.  Banks have begun to correct in the wake of strong outperformance, with investors taking the view that interest rates and consequently banks’ NIMs  are set to peak. NIMs had been a large driver of banks’ profitability in the past quarters.

 

Property also weighed on the index, underperforming despite the BSP’s decision to pause its rate hikes in the latest meeting.  

Although SM Prime’s mall revenue and reservation sales were similarly robust, the stock fell 3.7% due to a downweight in the MSCI Index.  Robinsons Land had a flat total return in May thanks to strong mall operations and residential reservation sales.

Filinvest Land dropped 10.1% MoM as its office vacancy climbed to a staggering 39% in 1Q23. Meanwhile, Vista Land’s (-2.8% MoM) share price fell as its residential revenue declined YoY for the 14th consecutive quarter.

 

Conglomerates were mixed. Liquid large cap SM Investments (+3.8% MoM) outperformed in May, as did Ayala Corp (+3.3% MoM). After raising c.US$600m from its value realization plans, Ayala Corp is targeting to raise another c.US$400m from the sale of non-core assets by the end of the year.

Topping the top index gainers list was GT Capital (+7.95% MoM) after 1Q23 results blew past expectations, attracting laggard interest.  Favorable FX and strong sales drove profits for the auto business to reach new highs.  

A shortfall in tobacco profits (-28%YoY) led to the underperformance of LT Group’s (-5.7% MoM) share price . Concerns about rising illicit trade and its impact to PMFTC’s cigarette sales could trim dividend expectations over the medium term.

MPI fell 1.8% MoM to end at P4.35/sh, below the tender offer price of P4.63/sh.  The strong 1Q23 results were largely ignored, as investors waited for the release of the final tender offer document, which may or may not lead to an adjustment in the offer price.

 

Telcos were mostly flat – with Globe unchanged and PLDT (-0.3% MoM) down slightly.  Both telcos reported 1Q23 numbers that featured sluggish revenue growth. For PLDT, service revenues were 4% higher YoY in 1Q, but mobile revenues actually contracted 1% in the quarter. In Globe’s case, service revenues were up 2% YoY,  though much of the growth came from non-telco segments.

Converge (-7.8% MoM) dropped.  While its 1Q323 net income appeared to be ahead of estimates, adjusting for unusually low costs would have put profits mildly behind. Adjusted revenue (normalized) in 1Q is estimated at 3% QoQ, better than the headline -6% QoQ but still modest.

Within the utilities space, First Gen delivered a notable 24.5% jump on the back of a sharp recovery in 1Q23 earnings (+58%). Its subsidiary also submitted the highest bid and was subsequently awarded the 165-MW Casecnan hydro facility in Nueva Ecija. The facility is envisioned to complement its existing hydro facility in Pantabangan.

Semirara (+3.7% MoM) rose following management’s confirmation of another chunky dividend payment this year.

Meanwhile, Manila Water (-6.1% MoM) fell after the government modified the FX pass-through provision on future loans.  The change could potentially raise funding costs and reduce the value of the East zone concession. 

 

 

 

 
MACRO AND POLITICAL NEWS

1Q23 GDP positively surprises at 6.4%. 1Q23 GDP came in at +6.4% YoY, higher than street estimates (6.2%) and decelerating from a revised 4Q22 GDP of 7.1% (previously 7.2%). This is well within the government’s target of 6-7% for FY23. On the demand side, consumption grew 6.3% YoY, slower than in 4Q (7.0%) but normalizing to historical trends. Private investment (ie. capital formation) rebounded, up 12.2% YoY (from 3.8% in 4%) and contributing 2.6ppts to GDP growth due to strong public construction. However, with export growth slowing sharply, net imports dragged GDP growth by 1.6ppts. On the supply side, all major economic sectors recorded positive growth. To reach Regis’ FY23E GDP growth target of 5.5%, GDP for the balance of the year should grow by 5.2%.

Inflation cools further to 6.6% in April. Headline CPI declined by 0.2% MoM and rose by 6.6% YoY. This is the slowest inflation rate in eight months and was below Bloomberg consensus forecast (7.2%); BSP forecast range: 6.3%-7.1%. Prices of food (vegetables, fish, and meat) and energy-related items (transport and electricity inflation decelerated further) continued to decline. Core CPI rose by 7.9% YoY, +0.3% MoM, moderately slowing from March (+8.0% YoY, +0.4% MoM). The YT-April average inflation rate is at 7.9%. The BSP’s 2023 inflation target at 6.0%; Regis forecast at 5.5%. To reach the BSP’s inflation target, CPI should rise by +0.5% MoM for the rest of the year. BSP monetary board is set to meet on May 18.

BSP pauses monetary tightening. The Monetary Board kept the interest rate on the overnight reverse repurchase facility at 6.25%,  in line with consensus expectations. The gap between the BSP’s policy rate and the Fed funds rate has narrowed to 1.25% from 1.5% previously. The gov’t cited (a) lower inflation expectations and (b) potential moderation in demand indicators in recent months. The BSP lowered its average inflation targets for 2023/2024 to 5.5%/2.8% from 6.0%/2.9% previously. BSP Governor Medalla said that they may continue to pause in the next 2-3 policy meetings. However, they will be mindful of the potential impact of El Nino and food prices and utility rates, as well as the soft global economy.

GIR steady at US$101.5bn in April. Preliminary data showed the GIR level settled at US$101.51bn in April, flattish MoM (-US$36.9mn). This represents 7.6 months’ worth of imports. The BSP expects the GIR to end at US$100bn this year.

 

BoP deficit narrows to US$148mn in April. The country’s overall balance of payments (BoP) position posted a deficit of US$148mn in April. This is lower than the US$415mn deficit in April 2022 but is a reversal of the US$1.27bn BOP surplus in March 2023. BSP cited outflows arising from the national government’s payments of foreign currency debt obligations. The cumulative 4M23 BoP position registered a surplus of US$3.3bn, higher than the US$79mn surplus in the same period last year.

Government records P66.8bn budget surplus in April. The budget surplus for April 2023 amounted to P66.8bn, up more than 13x YoY.  The surplus came as a result of revenue collections, which outpaced expenditures.  Revenues rose 27% YoY, with tax revenues up 32% YoY.  BIR collections rose 40% YoY while Customs registered a more modest growth of 2.9%. Expenditures grew 9% YoY, with primary expenditures up 7% YoY while interest payments rose 24% YoY.  The gov’t attributed the growth in primary spending to subsidy release to PhilHealth and expenditures related to public works. The latest print brings 4M23 budget deficit to P204.1bn, shrinking by 35% YoY and trending better than the government’s full-year deficit target. 

Maharlika Investment Fund Bill certified as urgent. President Marcos certified the enabling law for the Maharlika Investment Fund (MIF) as urgent. The US$1.4bn fund is expected to finance big government projects such as power grids and dams.

House adopts Senate version of Maharlika Bill. The House of Represntatives will adopt the Senate version of the Maharlika Investment Fund Bill. The bill will be transmitted to the Office of the President for signing into law.

Senate Bill No. 2020 has the following provisions: 

    • It allows the government financial institutions to pitch into the fund following approval of its board of directors, which will include the private sector
    • Land Bank and Development Bank of the Philippines will pitch in P50bn and P25bn
    • The national government will also contribute P50bn, which will come from dividend incomes from BSP, PAGCOR, and other royalties
    • This version also prohibits the use of funds from the pension funds (GSIS and SSS), Philhealth, Pag-IBIG, OWWA, PVAO in the capitalization
    • The Lower House’s version barred the Maharlika from taking on controlling stakes in its investments, but that provision was absent in the Senate’s iteration
  • The proposed MIF is primed to help bankroll the Marcos administration’s pipeline of 194 infrastructure flagship project.
 

U/KB loan growth steady at 10.1% YoY March. Preliminary data showed loans from universal and commercial banks (U/KBs) grew by 10.1% YoY in March. This is broadly the same as in Feb 2023: 10.0%. By production activities, loan growth to manufacturing, trade, electricity, and real estate accelerated vs. February. Consumer loans grew at a steady rate of 21% YoY. Meanwhile, Credit cards slowed to 27.9% YoY from 29.4%. Auto loans grew +0.5% after posting negative 1.3% growth in February. M3 growth was steady at 6.0% (unch MoM).

Vehicle sales drop 17% MoM in April. Vehicle sales, as reported by CAMPI, fell by 17% MoM to 30,643 units in April. On a YoY basis, vehicle sales were up 22%. Note that CAMPI began including Chery in Sep 2022. This brings 4M23 sales to 127,927 units, up 28% YoY (vs 2023E target of 395k, +12% YoY). Toyota sold 59,328 units in 4M23 (+16% YoY), implying that it sold 14,123 units in April (+3% YoY, -16% MoM). 

President Marcos signs deal extending Malampaya service contract. President Marcos Jr. signed an agreement renewing the service contract for the Malampaya gas field by 15 years or until 2039. Service Contract (SC) 38, which covers the Malampaya gas field in offshore Palawan, was originally scheduled to expire on Feb 22, 2024. “We optimistically look forward to the continued production and utilization of the remaining reserves of the Malampaya gas field, as well as further exploration and development of its untapped potential”. The Malampaya gas field is the country’s only indigenous source of natural gas and is expected to be commercially depleted by 2027. It supplies over 20% of the electricity requirements of the Luzon grid.

SC 38 is owned by the Malampaya consortium: Razon-led Prime Infrastructure (45% stake), UC38 LLC of the Udenna Group (45%), and PNOC-EC (10%). The consortium is mandated to conduct geological and geophysical studies and drilling of at least two deep water wells from 2024 to 2029. The consortium is also required to conduct exploratory drillings outside the Malampaya production area but still with the Service Contract to retain the exploration areas. SC38 has fueled gas plants owned by First Gen (FGEN PM) and San Miguel Global Power (1,200MW Ilijan, expired in 2022).
